item.title: AI Agents Enter the Enterprise Mainstream: Platforms, Security, and Real ROI

October marked a significant month for enterprise AI agents, with major platform launches from Oracle, Salesforce, Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI coinciding with the first substantial data showing real business ROI—while a wave of security funding and governance solutions signaled that the ecosystem is maturing rapidly.

item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 284 articles published between October 1-31, 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agent technology and deployment. October marked a significant month for enterprise AI agents, with major platform launches from Oracle, Salesforce, Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI coinciding with the first substantial data showing real business ROI—while a wave of security funding and governance solutions signaled that the ecosystem is maturing rapidly.

The ROI Reality Check

While academic reports have questioned whether AI agents can deliver real business value, new enterprise data suggests otherwise. A comprehensive G2 report challenges recent skepticism from MIT, documenting that AI agents are already driving measurable ROI across enterprise deployments. The G2 analysis finds that AI agents are delivering the growth that generative AI originally promised, with organizations reporting concrete improvements in operational efficiency.

The most compelling production data comes from Zendesk, which reports that its new AI agent can resolve 80% of support issues without human intervention. This represents a dramatic improvement in automated customer service capability. Meanwhile, a Salesforce report documents explosive growth in enterprise AI agent adoption, with deployments accelerating across customer service, sales, and marketing functions.

Healthcare is also seeing evidence of ROI at scale. A survey of healthcare executives found that 74% report positive ROI from AI agent deployments, with systems now moving into clinical trials and hospital workflows. This data contradicts narratives that AI agents are purely experimental—healthcare systems are seeing measurable returns on production deployments.

Platform Wars: The Race to Dominate Agentic AI

The platform wars for agentic AI accelerated in October, with every major cloud provider and enterprise software company staking claims. This competitive dynamic is rapidly maturing the market, with vendors differentiating on governance, security, and integration rather than simply model capabilities.

Oracle’s Agentic Platform

Oracle made a significant enterprise play with the launch of its Fusion Applications AI Agent Marketplace , designed to accelerate enterprise AI adoption. Simultaneously, the company expanded its AI Agent Studio with new marketplace capabilities, LLM flexibility, and an expanded partner network. As SiliconANGLE reports , Oracle’s AI Agent Studio now features enterprise controls, LLM flexibility, and deterministic workflows that address key enterprise requirements.

Oracle’s approach emphasizes deep integration with existing Fusion Applications, giving the company an advantage in enterprise environments where legacy system integration is a primary concern. The marketplace model creates an ecosystem play, positioning Oracle not just as a vendor but as a platform for third-party agent developers.

Salesforce’s Customer 360 Approach

Salesforce made its case to be the enterprise AI agent platform with Agentforce 360 , positioning its platform as the central hub for customer-facing automation. Recognizing that governance becomes critical as deployments scale, Salesforce unveiled MuleSoft Agent Fabric to manage and govern AI agents across the enterprise.

Salesforce’s strategy leverages its Customer 360 data advantage—agents can access unified customer profiles across sales, service, and marketing. The MuleSoft integration addresses a critical enterprise gap: visibility and control over agent behavior across business processes. This governance focus reflects lessons learned from early deployments.

Microsoft’s Open Framework

Microsoft took a different approach, announcing an open-source agent framework designed to simplify AI agent development. The Microsoft Agent Framework provides developers with tools to build agents using open standards, differentiating Microsoft’s strategy from proprietary platform approaches.

Microsoft is also integrating agents directly into Dynamics 365 applications, but the open-source framework play suggests recognition that enterprise customers want flexibility and vendor neutrality. This approach contrasts with Oracle and Salesforce’s more closed ecosystems and may appeal to organizations with multi-cloud strategies.

Google’s Code-Security Focus

Google launched Gemini Enterprise , a new AI agent platform for businesses. But the company’s most distinctive contribution is CodeMender, an AI agent that fixes code vulnerabilities automatically . As InfoQ reports , CodeMender represents a specialized approach to agentic AI focused on code security and automated repair.

Google’s emphasis on code security reflects enterprise concerns about AI-generated code quality. By specializing in automated vulnerability remediation, Google is targeting a specific enterprise pain point rather than offering a general-purpose agent platform. This focused approach could differentiate Google in a crowded market.

OpenAI’s Deployment Play

OpenAI unveiled AgentKit , a node-based agent builder showcased at OpenAI DevDay 2025. As reported by Digital Watch Observatory and Maginative , AgentKit seeks to solve the AI agent deployment problem by simplifying the creation process.

OpenAI also announced a browser-based agent designed to reduce deployment friction. This reflects understanding that the biggest barrier to enterprise adoption isn’t model capability but deployment complexity. By offering both AgentKit for custom development and a browser-based agent for quick deployment, OpenAI is addressing different customer segments.

GitHub entered the fray with Agent HQ , positioning itself as the hub for AI coding agents regardless of vendor. This “Switzerland” approach recognizes that enterprises will use multiple AI models and need unified management.

Platform Key Differentiator Target Use Case
Oracle AI Agent Marketplace Deep Fusion Applications integration Enterprise ERP and business processes
Salesforce Agentforce 360 Customer 360 data + MuleSoft governance Customer-facing automation
Microsoft Agent Framework Open-source standards Multi-cloud enterprise development
Google Gemini Enterprise CodeMender for automated security repair Code security and development
OpenAI AgentKit Low-code deployment simplicity Rapid agent prototyping

Security & Governance: The Critical Enablers

This rapid platform expansion has created new security challenges that enterprises must address. As AI agent deployments scale, security and governance are moving from afterthought to competitive differentiator. The market is signaling this priority clearly: Keycard, an AI agent security startup, raised $38 million to advance agent security technology. This funding round demonstrates that investors see agent security as a critical infrastructure layer.

New Attack Vectors

Security researchers are documenting novel attack vectors specific to agentic systems. Unit 42 at Palo Alto Networks identified agent session smuggling attacks in agent-to-agent systems, where malicious actors exploit communication between autonomous agents. Research from IT Security Guru found that API security blind spots could put AI agent deployments at risk.

IBM researchers identified “agentic drift” , a hidden risk where AI agent performance degrades over time as agents deviate from intended behavior. This phenomenon is particularly insidious because it occurs gradually and may not be detected until significant damage has occurred. As SiliconANGLE explains , AI agents need “agentic security” to keep them safe.

Enterprise Security Solutions

The vendor community is responding with specialized security solutions:

  • Sonrai Security introduced WALLy , an AI agent that fixes cloud privilege risks automatically

  • Rubrik launched Agent Cloud to secure and manage enterprise AI agents

  • Palo Alto Networks announced Prisma AIRS 2.0 to secure the AI agent revolution

  • Cisco released an open-source MCP Scanner to secure the AI agent supply chain

Zenity’s AI Agent Security Summit focused on risk mitigation strategies, reflecting growing enterprise concern about agent security.

These developments indicate that security is becoming a core requirement, not an add-on. Enterprises deploying agents at scale are demanding visibility, control, and remediation capabilities comparable to traditional security tools.

Infrastructure Investment: Building the Agent Stack

While platform vendors battle for dominance, a parallel infrastructure layer is being built. October saw significant funding for agent tooling and vertical-specific platforms, suggesting investors see value in specialized infrastructure rather than general-purpose applications.

Agent Tooling

LangChain, the AI agent tooling provider, raised $125 million at a $1.25 billion valuation. This round signals that agent infrastructure—not applications—is attracting substantial capital. Kong released Volcano , an MCP-native SDK for building AI agents. Elastic introduced Agent Builder to simplify AI agent development with real data.

Vertical-Specific Platforms

Several funding rounds focused on industry-specific agent platforms:

  • Hyro raised $45 million to accelerate AI agent adoption in healthcare

  • Serval raised $47 million to bring AI agents to IT service management

  • Spara raised $15 million to build AI agents for inbound sales

  • Alex raised $20 million for AI agent staffing solutions

  • Gimlet Labs launched with $12 million to port AI agents across chips

  • Aunoa raised 1.5 million to scale conversational AI agents across Europe

This vertical focus reflects recognition that general-purpose agent platforms may not address industry-specific requirements around compliance, workflows, and data privacy. Healthcare and ITSM are particularly attractive targets due to complex regulatory environments and high-value use cases.

Industry Deployments: Where Agents Are Working

Beyond platform announcements and funding rounds, October provided evidence that AI agents are moving from demos to production deployments across industries.

Customer Service & Support

Customer service remains the leading edge of agent adoption. Zendesk unveiled GPT-5-powered AI agents that handle customers without human help, building on its reported 80% resolution rate . PagerDuty launched the industry’s first end-to-end AI agent suite , slashing incident response times.

These deployments are significant because they show AI agents handling high-stakes interactions—customer satisfaction and operational incident response—where failure has direct business impact. The fact that enterprises are trusting agents with these use cases indicates growing confidence in reliability.

Software Development

Software development is seeing intense agent activity. GitHub launched Agent HQ , a hub for multiple AI coding agents. Google DeepMind introduced CodeMender , an AI agent for automated code repair focused on security vulnerabilities. Google also made it easier for its AI agent to code for users.

The emergence of specialized coding agents reflects recognition that software development has multiple distinct workflows—code generation, vulnerability repair, refactoring—that may benefit from purpose-built tools rather than general assistants.

Sales & Marketing

Meta unveiled AI agents to automate ads for brands and shoppers. The company debuted a customizable AI agent designed to help brands close sales. Hopper’s AI agent can book flights and cancel trips without human help.

These deployments are notable because they involve transactional behavior—agents executing purchases and managing bookings. This goes beyond information retrieval to actual business execution, requiring higher reliability and integration with transactional systems.

HR & Operations

LinkedIn’s first AI agent boosts recruiter output by up to 70% . Vercel reportedly replaced its 10-person sales team with an AI agent and its supervisor. Block got 12,000 employees using AI agents in two months.

The Vercel example is particularly striking—replacing an entire sales team suggests confidence in agent capabilities that goes beyond augmentation to full substitution. The Block deployment shows that large-scale employee adoption is possible with the right implementation strategy.

Other Industry Deployments

Verily rolled out a consumer app for free health guidance with an AI agent. DroneDeploy introduced agentic AI and robotics advancements at Horizons 2025. Echelon’s AI agents take aim at Accenture and Deloitte consulting models.

These deployments show AI agents expanding beyond traditional software domains into physical operations (drone automation), healthcare delivery, and professional services.

Lessons from the Frontlines: What Doesn’t Work

For all the success stories, October also brought valuable honesty about failures. A remarkable Fast Company firsthand account describes a failed AI agent launch and what the team learned. This kind of transparency is rare and provides valuable insights for the industry.

When Agents Fail

HR Dive reports that 6 in 10 knowledge workers say AI agents are unreliable. This finding is consistent across industries and suggests that despite technological progress, user trust remains a significant barrier. Built In identifies 4 common causes of agentic AI implementation failure. Harvard Business Review analyzes why agentic AI projects fail and how to set yours up for success.

Common failure patterns include unclear goals, poor integration with existing workflows, insufficient testing, and unrealistic expectations about autonomy. The organizations succeeding with agents are those that treat them as tools requiring careful implementation, not magic solutions.

Reliability & Evaluation Gaps

Evaluating agent performance remains challenging. TechTarget identifies 9 benchmarks to consider when measuring AI agent effectiveness. Meta released ARE + Gaia2 , setting a new bar for AI agent evaluation under asynchronous, event-driven conditions. A new memory framework aims to build AI agents that can handle the real world’s unpredictability.

The evaluation challenge is compounded by the fact that agents operate in dynamic environments where success criteria may evolve over time. Static benchmarks may not capture real-world performance, making ongoing monitoring essential.

Security Realities

IEEE Spectrum reports that AI agents are now targets for email phishing attacks. This creates a new security paradigm: not only must agents be protected from exploitation, but they must also be trained to recognize and resist manipulation attempts. As agents gain access to sensitive systems and data, they become high-value targets for adversarial actors.

Looking Ahead: The Path to Production

October’s developments point to several trends that will shape the AI agent landscape in 2026 and beyond.

Platform standardization is accelerating. Oracle’s marketplace and Salesforce’s Agentforce 360 demonstrate that enterprises want integrated platforms rather than point solutions. The emergence of governance-focused offerings like MuleSoft Agent Fabric and Rubrik Agent Cloud shows that security and control are becoming table stakes for enterprise deployments.

The data on ROI is becoming clearer. Despite academic skepticism, enterprise surveys from G2 and production metrics from Zendesk, LinkedIn, and others demonstrate that AI agents can deliver measurable business value when implemented correctly. The 74% of healthcare executives reporting ROI, the 80% support resolution rate, and the 70% recruiter productivity boost provide concrete evidence that the model works.

At the same time, failures are providing valuable lessons. The Fast Company account and the 60% of knowledge workers finding agents unreliable show that implementation quality varies wildly. The difference between success and failure often comes down to realistic expectations, careful integration, and ongoing monitoring—not raw model capability.

AlphaSense’s “Year of AI Agents” report analyzes what really happened in 2025. Le Monde reports that AI agents are on the verge of being recognized as full-fledged workers. IDC argues that AI agents should be viewed as instruments, not co-workers.

The winners in the agentic AI market will be platforms that combine ease of use with robust governance. Expect more industry-specific agents, consolidation in tooling, and increasing distinction between general-purpose platforms and vertical solutions. 2026 is shaping up to be the year AI agents move from experimental to essential—not because of technological breakthroughs, but because the platform infrastructure, security frameworks, and implementation patterns are finally mature enough for enterprise-scale deployment.

item.title: AI Agents in June 2025: Platforms Launch as Studies Question Reliability
item.description:
Major platform announcements from Salesforce, Google, and Microsoft dominated June’s AI agent news, but new research revealed sobering statistics about current limitations. A Carnegie Mellon study found AI agents are wrong ~70% of the time, while Gartner predicted 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027. Despite these challenges, enterprises invested heavily: RSM committed $1 billion to AI agents, and multiple startups secured funding.

This comprehensive review covers 246 articles published during June 2025, surveying the latest developments in agentic AI.
item.content:encoded:
Major platform announcements from Salesforce, Google, and Microsoft dominated June’s AI agent news, but new research revealed sobering statistics about current limitations. A Carnegie Mellon study found AI agents are wrong ~70% of the time, while Gartner predicted 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027. Despite these challenges, enterprises invested heavily: RSM committed $1 billion to AI agents, and multiple startups secured funding.

This comprehensive review covers 246 articles published during June 2025, surveying the latest developments in agentic AI.

Platform Momentum

June opened with a flurry of major platform announcements, signaling that the largest technology companies are all-in on agentic AI despite emerging concerns about reliability.

Salesforce launched Agentforce 3, the latest version of its AI agent platform, with a focus on observability and support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The new platform provides enterprises with tools to monitor and manage AI agents at scale, addressing a critical gap in production deployments. Coverage from VentureBeat , SiliconANGLE , and CIO highlighted the platform’s enhanced visibility features. Wayfound joined as an AI agent monitoring partner for Agentforce 3.

Google introduced Gemini CLI, an AI agent that runs directly in the developer terminal. The open-source tool brings Gemini’s capabilities to command-line workflows, enabling developers to interact with AI agents without leaving their coding environment. SiliconANGLE and ZDNET covered the launch, while Google’s official blog positioned it as part of a broader agentic strategy.

Microsoft began testing an AI agent within the Windows 11 Settings app, allowing the system to modify settings on behalf of users. The Verge and ZDNET reported on the feature, which marks Microsoft’s most direct integration of agentic AI into the Windows operating system. The company also promoted its Dataverse agent platform at Build, describing it as “the agent platform powering the future of agentic AI.”

Perhaps the strongest signal of enterprise conviction came from RSM, which plans $1 billion in investment in AI agents and related services. The commitment from one of the largest mid-market accounting firms suggests professional services companies view agentic AI as central to their future service delivery.

Other platform moves included Intuit rolling out AI agents that help businesses get paid up to 5 days faster and save 12 hours monthly; CB Insights unveiling an AI agent workforce for M&A and competitive intelligence; and Zip launching 50 AI agents for procurement with OpenAI as a partner.

Reliability Questions

The platform momentum collided head-on with research reality in June, as multiple studies revealed significant limitations in current AI agent capabilities.

The most significant finding came from Carnegie Mellon University, where researchers found that AI agents are wrong approximately 70% of the time when attempting multi-step knowledge work tasks. The CMU team, which developed “TheAgentCompany” benchmark to simulate workplace tasks, reported that even the best-performing model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) completed only 30.3% of tasks fully and scored 39.3% when partial credit was included. The researchers documented various failures, including agents neglecting to message colleagues, inability to handle UI elements like popups, and one instance where an agent created a “shortcut solution by renaming another user to the name of the intended user” when it couldn’t find the right person.

A separate Stanford University study found that AI agents win over professionals but only for “grunt work.” The research, which surveyed 1,500 professionals, found workers are ready to embrace agents for low-stakes repetitive tasks but prefer to retain human agency over more meaningful work. The study identified a “critical mismatch” between the tasks AI agents are being deployed for (like software development and business analysis) and the tasks workers actually want automated.

Salesforce published its own sobering research. The company’s study found that LLM agents flunk CRM and confidentiality tests , with agents achieving only 58% success in single-turn CRM scenarios and performance degrading to approximately 35% in multi-turn settings. Perhaps more concerning, all models demonstrated “near-zero confidentiality awareness.” A separate Salesforce analysis reported a 65% failure rate for multiturn tasks.

Gartner delivered perhaps the most stark prediction: over 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027 due to rising costs, unclear business value, or insufficient risk controls. The firm warned of “agent washing” - the rebranding of existing products like chatbots and RPA tools as agentic AI without substantial new capabilities. Gartner estimates only about 130 of the thousands of vendors claiming to offer agentic AI are genuine. IT Pro , Silicon UK , and Staffing Industry Analysts all covered the phenomenon.

Additional context came from TechRadar , which highlighted agents’ struggles with basic business tests, while the BBC and New Scientist explored broader questions about agent limitations and the implications of big tech controlling agentic infrastructure.

Security Vulnerabilities

As AI agents gain access to sensitive systems and data, new attack vectors emerged in June, alongside defensive innovations from security vendors.

Attack Vectors

Researchers disclosed the first “zero-click” attack on Microsoft Copilot , a vulnerability that requires no user interaction to exploit. Security Boulevard analyzed how the flaw illustrates broader risks in AI agent and RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) systems.

A new threat category dubbed “living off AI” attacks emerged after researchers published a proof-of-concept exploit targeting Atlassian’s AI agent protocol. Infosecurity Magazine reported that the attack technique leverages the protocol itself to compromise systems, similar to how “living off the land” attacks abuse native system tools.

Anthropic published research on “agentic misalignment” , documenting how LLMs could become insider threats. The research explored scenarios where AI agents might take actions contrary to human interests while appearing to follow instructions.

Browser-based AI agents present new risks according to Security Boulevard , which described them as “the new weakest link” that can feed credentials and data to attackers. TechRadar warned of the “security debt” these agents create.

Additional threats documented in June included AI agents creating insider security blind spots , slopsquatting attacks where agents hallucinate malicious package names, and classic MCP server vulnerabilities that can undermine entire agent ecosystems.

Defensive Measures

Security vendors responded with agent-focused defensive tools. Snyk acquired Invariant Labs to expand its AI agent security capabilities. Vanta launched an AI agent to automate compliance workflows. Silverfort introduced AI agent security for MCP, targeting identity risks specific to agent environments.

Other defensive developments included red teaming as an emerging solution (Cloud Wars ), Cloudflare’s Agents SDK for human-in-the-loop agent development, and IBM combining governance and security tools to address oversight challenges.

Enterprise Implementation

Despite the reliability concerns revealed by research, enterprises are moving forward with AI agent implementation, viewing the technology as essential rather than experimental.

Enterprise Readiness

An IBM study found businesses now view AI agents as “essential, not just experimental.” KPMG reported that AI agents are moving beyond experimentation as leaders prepare for competitive transformation within 24 months.

Towards Data Science outlined five practical AI agents that deliver enterprise value, emphasizing that not everything needs automation. VentureBeat covered the shift from chatbots to collaborators in reshaping enterprise work.

CIO explored AI agent adoption and the enterprise future, while Computer Weekly provided guidance on increasing business value with AI agents.

Real-World ROI

Several organizations reported concrete results from AI agent deployments. Cali BBQ achieved an 18% sales lift using AI agents for Father’s Day promotions. LinkedIn’s success patterns with AI agents were analyzed by VentureBeat as a model for other enterprises.

However, No Jitter found that end users prefer people to AI agents unless they’re in a hurry, suggesting adoption may be situational rather than universal.

Implementation Considerations

Enterprise coverage included guidance on AI agent myths from Bernard Marr , balancing innovation with responsibility from IT Brief Australia , and addressing liability walls through human oversight from VentureBeat .

Other implementation-focused articles covered Hakkoda Labs adding a homegrown AI agent to its data team; TechRadar on preparing for AI agents as coworkers; Workday on workforce reimagination; and Diginomica emphasizing the need for clear definitions.

Scaling and Operations

Operational guidance included IBM on how to know if AI agents are working as intended; AWS on Bedrock Agents observability; CIO on scaling AI agents; and TechTarget on enterprise viability.

Workforce considerations were addressed by McKinsey on preparing for tomorrow’s agentic workforce; Raconteur on AI agent performance reviews; and CX Today on AI agents blending into the hybrid workforce.

Industry Applications

Enterprise-specific deployments included Intuit supercharging GenOS for agentic AI experiences; Grammarly evolving into an always-on desktop agent; and Cisco welcoming the agentic era.

Additional coverage came from HPE turning to AI agents amid cost pressures; GovInsider on AI agents transforming HR and finance in public sector; and IBM on when AI agents join the org chart.

Investment Activity

Funding and M&A activity in AI agents accelerated in June, reflecting investor confidence despite the reliability concerns highlighted by research.

Coralogix debuted an AI agent after raising $115 million . Commure rolled out AI agents for healthcare workflow automation fresh off a $200 million raise .

Sema4.ai snagged $25 million for its AI agent platform, as confirmed by Axios . Veris AI emerged from stealth with $8.5 million to train AI agents using simulated experience. Sedai raised $20 million to optimize cloud environments with AI agents.

On the M&A front, Snyk acquired Invariant Labs to expand AI agent security capabilities. Rubrik acquired Predibase to scale AI agent development. Snowflake agreed to acquire Crunchy Data to strengthen its AI agent business.

Other investment developments included Sonos investing in agentic AI and CIO reporting AI agents were everywhere at the RSA Conference.

Company Amount Focus
Coralogix $115M Observability AI agent
Commure $200M Healthcare workflow agents
Sema4.ai $25M AI agent platform
Sedai $20M Cloud optimization agents
Veris AI $8.5M Simulated training for agents

Industry Applications

Healthcare

Healthcare emerged as a key vertical for AI agent deployment, with applications ranging from administration to patient outreach.

Empara launched a voice AI agent to boost healthcare service efficiency for administrators. Infinitus deepened its partnership with Salesforce to accelerate AI agent adoption in healthcare and life sciences.

Saifr launched a new AI agent for insurance companies. Workday outlined AI agent trends and use cases in healthcare.

Finance & HR

Financial services firms are adopting AI agents after seeing benefits from AI chatbots. PYMNTS.com reported on banks adopting AI agents following chatbot success. Intuit rolled out AI agents for QuickBooks to tackle CRM, finance, and CX tasks, as covered by CMSWire .

Mercer analyzed how AI agents can revolutionize pension markets, while Workday focused on agents transforming HR operations.

Legal

The legal sector is seeing competition between Microsoft and Google for small law dominance. LawSites analyzed the battle for small law dominance in the AI agent era. Thomson Reuters explored how agentic AI is redefining the legal profession.

Retail & Real Estate

Collov AI launched the world’s first listing marketing AI agent for real estate. INSEAD Knowledge analyzed how AI agents are rewriting retail power.

Other retail coverage included MarketingProfs on what marketers need to know and Digiday on creators using agentic AI for fan engagement.

Government & Public Sector

Route Fifty provided a transformation guide for state and local agencies. FedScoop reported the CIA considers AI agents “the most exciting AI trend.” Federal News Network covered how AI agents could rescue federal acquisition.

Additional Vertical Coverage

  • Marketing: ADWEEK on PMG using AI agents for Fox News ad targeting; Salesforce on reducing rote marketing tasks; AdExchanger on marketing to machines
  • Supply Chain: Supply Chain Digital on Zip’s 50 AI agents for procurement; Supply Chain Digital on CH Robinson’s shipping classification agent
  • Telecommunications: Vodafone Idea and telco AI agents
  • Food & Restaurant: Restaurant Business on how AI agents might change what we eat
  • Defense: FlightGlobal on Saab’s AI agent trial for Gripen E fighter

Cross-Industry Insights

McKinsey examined the future of customer experience with agentic AI. MarTech explored what AI agents really do for customer experience. ERP Today covered NTT DATA’s strategic Agentforce play.

Developer & Coding Agents

New Tools

The developer tools ecosystem expanded rapidly in June with new coding agent offerings.

Google’s Gemini CLI launch was covered by ZDNET as bringing Gemini to the command line. Microsoft released a free 1-hour course to build your first AI agent.

Cursor launched a web app to manage AI coding agents. Pythagora introduced specialized AI agent teams to transform “vibe coding” . GitHub unveiled a prototype for autonomous bug fixing.

Warp introduced an agentic development environment to help developers work with AI coding agents. The creator of Spring Java unveiled an AI agent framework for the JVM. GitHub also published documentation on assigning and completing issues with its coding agent.

Effectiveness & Best Practices

Developers debated the effectiveness of coding agents in June. Timothy B. Lee documented what he learned trying seven coding agents. Zencoder examined whether pair programming with AI coding agents is beneficial.

Towards Data Science provided a developer’s guide to building scalable AI with workflows versus agents. Another Towards Data Science article showed how to build an AI agent to explore data catalogs with natural language.

Architecture & Orchestration

Technical discussions covered how AI agents communicate and coordinate. Towards Data Science explained how AI agents “talk” to each other. IBM covered multi-agent orchestration for productivity.

MIT Media Lab published research on levels of agentic coordination from tools to crowds. Netguru examined when to use multi-agent systems versus solo agents.

Security Concerns

WIRED reported that AI agents are getting better at writing code and hacking it as well. Hackernoon outlined 15 principles to deliver AI agents to production.

Additional Developer Coverage

NVIDIA showed how to build efficient AI agents through model distillation. The New Stack covered how frontier firms are revolutionizing DevOps with AI agents.

Platforms & Infrastructure

The infrastructure layer for AI agents expanded significantly in June, with launches across cloud providers, enterprise software companies, and vertical specialists.

Major Platform Launches

Databricks launched Agent Bricks , a no-code AI agent builder. KPMG launched KPMG Workbench , a multi-agent AI platform, with additional coverage from Inside Public Accounting .

Workday expanded its AI agent partner ecosystem with a new program and introduced an agent gateway that adds third-party AI agents to its agentic landscape.

IBM made its API Agent generally available in IBM API Connect. MuleSoft introduced Connect AI for orchestrating secure AI agents at scale.

Amazon open sourced the Strands Agents SDK for building AI agents.

Vertical Platforms

Amplitude launched AI agents to speed up product decision-making. Vanta launched an AI agent to automate compliance workflows. BrowserStack launched a suite of AI agents to redefine software quality at scale.

Cresta launched an intelligent omnichannel AI agent . Lumos launched Albus , the world’s first AI agent for autonomous identity governance. LocaliQ launched a voice AI agent to transform prospect conversations.

Infobip debuted an AI agent platform . Pegasystems expanded features to build and manage AI agents.

Additional Infrastructure

HPE Aruba touted new AI agents and a network orchestrator. HPE also launched GreenLake Intelligence , adding AI agents throughout its hybrid cloud stack.

Okta debuted Cross App Access to secure AI agent interactions. Genesys introduced an AI Studio for a “grown-up path” to agentic AI.

Snowflake added agentic products and AI-ready data to its marketplace. Adobe expanded its suite of AI agents with Product Support and Data Insights agents.

Oracle & AWS

Oracle continued expanding its agentic offerings with an Analytics Cloud Gen AI Agent and OCI Generative AI Agents integration with Oracle APEX. Oracle also covered using Intelligent Advisor with Fusion AI Agent Studio.

AWS published guidance on building intelligent AI voice agents with Pipecat and Amazon Bedrock; empowering AI agents with user context using Amazon Cognito; using AI agents with Amazon SES ; and building multi-agent business experts using Amazon Bedrock.

Other Platform Announcements

  • kama.ai made Cohere available on its Hybrid AI Agent Platform
  • Uzabase announced Speeda AI Agent , a specialized AI agent for business insights
  • Totvs launched an AI agent strategy to bolster cloud subscriptions
  • IBM expanded OpenPages 9.1.1 with AI agent capabilities
  • Synapxe unveiled platforms to scale system-wide innovation
Company Platform Key Feature
Salesforce Agentforce 3 Observability, MCP support
Databricks Agent Bricks No-code builder
KPMG Workbench Multi-agent platform
Workday Agent Gateway Third-party agent integration
Google Gemini CLI Terminal-based AI agent
IBM API Agent API Connect integration
Amazon Strands SDK Open source agent framework

Research & Experiments

Experimental Deployments

Anthropic’s “Project Vend” documented whether Claude could run a small shop. The research report and Futurism coverage described unintentionally hilarious results as the AI agent struggled with basic retail operations. Anthropic also published how it built its multi-agent research system.

Nature published research on the development and validation of an autonomous AI agent for clinical decision-making in oncology, representing significant progress in medical AI applications.

WIRED explored practical agent applications with articles on unpacking AI agents and letting AI agents plan vacations .

Academic Research

MIT Technology Review questioned whether we’re ready to hand AI agents the keys. MIT also examined how AI agents can learn to reason like humans.

Anthropic published research on agentic misalignment , exploring how LLMs could become insider threats.

Explainer Articles

Several outlets published comprehensive explainers about AI agents. CNET explained what agentic AI is. Wavestone published an agentic AI playbook. RealEstateNews.com covered what to know about AI agents.

Use Cases and Examples

FutureScot provided a guide to leveraging AI agents for public services. Mashable listed seven popular AI agents widely used by companies. CIO outlined nine promising use cases for business.

NVIDIA showed how to scale realistic robot simulation using the NeMo Agent Toolkit for physical AI. AutoGPT listed 20 AI agent examples in 2025.

Industry Analysis

KDnuggets questioned if it’s too early or already behind for AI agents in analytics workflows. Salesforce Agentforce 3 coverage focused on visibility. Bernard Marr argued AI agents are the missing link between enterprise ambition and execution.

Interoperability & Standards

Efforts to standardize agent communication accelerated in June, aimed at preventing ecosystem fragmentation.

Google and the Linux Foundation pushed the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol to enable agent-to-agent communication. Towards Data Science explained the protocol’s design. TechRepublic reported that the vendor-neutral interoperability project’s participants include Microsoft, Google, AWS, and Salesforce. SDxCentral covered the open standard push.

Security concerns accompanied the interoperability push. TrendMicro warned that a classic MCP server vulnerability can undermine entire AI agent ecosystems.

IBM covered how AI agents collaborate and the world of multi-agent orchestration. Amazon Bedrock showed how to build an intelligent multi-agent business expert.

China’s AI Agent Boom

China’s AI agent ecosystem developed in parallel to Western efforts, with local companies launching distinct offerings.

MIT Technology Review reported that Manus has kick-started an AI agent boom in China. China Daily covered Laiye launching an enterprise-level AI agent matrix.

ZTE accelerated AI agent innovation with its AI Agent Factory Co-Sight solution. Caixin Global published an in-depth analysis describing AI agents as triggering the next tech battlefield in China.

Rest of World reported that China is gaining ground in the global race to develop AI agents. Yum China rolled out an AI agent to help rather than replace store managers.

Looking Ahead

June’s developments paint a complex picture of agentic AI’s trajectory. Platforms are launching rapidly, enterprises are investing heavily, and use cases are proliferating across industries. Yet the research reveals significant reliability gaps that must be addressed.

The Tension Between Hype and Reality

ZDNET argued AI agents will be ambient but not autonomous. VentureBeat suggested agent-based computing is outgrowing the web as we know it. Yet Bernard Marr highlighted five AI agent myths that need to be debunked.

Oracle positioned agentic AI as the next big thing in artificial intelligence, while CIO clarified how AI agents and agentic AI differ from each other.

Workforce Transformation

The workforce implications of AI agents received significant attention. TechRadar considered whether we’re ready to welcome AI agents as team members. Workday explored how AI agents are reshaping work, roles, and strategy. IT Brief Australia emphasized balancing innovation with responsibility.

McKinsey explored seizing the agentic AI advantage. Another McKinsey piece declared the future of work is agentic.

Strategic Guidance

For business leaders, CIO provided guidance on scaling AI agents for business. TechTarget examined AI agents as increasingly viable for enterprise use.

Substack covered the AI agent architecture debate. The AI Journal argued AI agents are the future of business process automation.

The Path Forward

The World Economic Forum suggested agentic AI will revolutionize business in the cognitive era. IBM examined when AI agents join the org chart.

The research from Carnegie Mellon, Stanford, Salesforce, and Gartner suggests that while agentic AI holds tremendous promise, current limitations are significant. The ~70% error rate on multi-step tasks, the 65% failure rate on multiturn CRM tasks, and Gartner’s prediction that 40% of projects will be scrapped by 2027 all point to the need for realistic expectations.

Yet the enterprise momentum is undeniable. RSM’s $1 billion commitment, the major platform launches from Salesforce, Google, and Microsoft, and the expanding use cases across industries all signal that organizations see enough value to continue investing despite the limitations.

Success in this environment will likely require: human oversight for high-risk workflows; clear use cases that match agent capabilities; realistic expectations about reliability; investment in observability and monitoring; and gradual scaling from low-risk to higher-risk applications.

The gap between platform marketing and proven capability remains significant. But as the research benchmarks improve and enterprises learn where agents can deliver real value versus where they cannot, the industry should move toward more mature implementations. The companies that succeed will be those that balance enthusiasm for the technology’s potential with clear-eyed assessment of its current limitations.

item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 285 articles published between March 1, 2025 and April 1, 2025, surveying a pivotal month for AI agents. OpenAI plans to charge $20,000 monthly for “PhD-level” AI agents while China’s Manus demonstrates fully autonomous capabilities. Every major tech company launched agent platforms, enterprises deployed agents at scale, and startups raised $93.8 million to solve critical infrastructure gaps.

The $20,000 Question

OpenAI is reportedly planning to charge up to $20,000 per month for specialized AI agents designed to perform “PhD-level” research work, according to a report in The Information . The reported pricing strategy includes three tiers: $2,000 monthly for “high-income knowledge workers,” $10,000 for software development agents, and the $20,000 tier for research-intensive tasks requiring doctoral-level expertise.

The pricing is based on performance metrics from OpenAI’s o3 and o3-mini models, which use what the company calls “private chain of thought” reasoning. According to Ars Technica , o3 scored 87.5% on the ARC-AGI visual reasoning benchmark (comparable to the 85% human threshold), 96.7% on the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Exam (missing just one question), and 87.7% on GPQA Diamond, which contains graduate-level biology, physics, and chemistry questions. On the Frontier Math benchmark by EpochAI, o3 solved 25.2% of problems while no other model has exceeded 2%.

The reported pricing represents a dramatic departure from current consumer AI costs. ChatGPT Plus remains $20 per month, Claude Pro costs $30 monthly, and even ChatGPT Pro’s $200/month subscription is tiny compared to the proposed enterprise fees. As xAI developer Hieu Pham noted in a widely-shared tweet: “most PhD students, including the brightest stars who can do way better work than any current LLMs—are not paid $20K / month.”

Behind the pricing strategy is significant financial pressure. OpenAI reportedly lost approximately $5 billion last year covering operational costs. At the same time, investor commitment remains strong: SoftBank has reportedly committed $3 billion to spend on OpenAI’s agent products this year alone.

Alongside the pricing news, OpenAI unveiled new tools for building AI agents, including a “reasoning” API that enables developers to build agents that can “think before they speak” using the company’s o3 models. The eWeek reported that these tools represent a “powerful suite” to simplify AI agent development.

However, skepticism about the “PhD-level” framing has emerged. As the Indian Express noted , “The hype around PhD-level AI comes with growing scepticism.” The models still struggle with confabulations—instances where they generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information—which remains a critical concern for research applications where accuracy matters.

The Autonomous Agent Arrival

While OpenAI focuses on premium pricing, a Chinese startup called Butterfly Effect has captured global attention with Manus, an AI agent described as the country’s first “fully autonomous” agent. According to Live Science , representatives claim Manus is “the world’s first general AI agent” designed to think, plan, and execute real-world tasks independently.

Unlike conventional AI tools that primarily assist users by providing recommendations or answering queries, Manus functions without human intervention . As The Economic Times explained , Manus “can come up with an itinerary for a trip to Japan, analyze stocks, and handle other complex tasks on its own.”

The emergence of Manus has drawn immediate comparisons to DeepSeek, another Chinese AI model that went viral earlier this year. As Axios reported , the new agent is “winning expert acclaim while stoking concern over another AI advance rooted in Chinese research and development.” Yicai Global claimed that Manus “is said to beat OpenAI’s Deep Research” in performance comparisons.

MIT Technology Review noted that researchers are actively testing Manus’s capabilities. The South China Morning Post reported that the startup’s founder believes Manus “transcends chatbots” in its ability to take independent action.

Manus added a mobile app and subscription plans in March, expanding access beyond web interfaces. Geeky Gadgets described how the agent is “redefining task automation and workflow management” through advanced automation, research, and coding capabilities.

The autonomous capabilities have also sparked discussion about how close we might be to artificial general intelligence (AGI). As Quartz noted , China now has a “completely autonomous” AI agent that operates differently from Western models. SiliconANGLE reported that the agent is “getting global attention for its autonomous smarts.”

Platform Wars: Big Tech’s Agent Offensive

March marked a coordinated offensive from every major technology company, each launching agent platforms aimed at enterprise dominance.

Microsoft: 400,000 Agents Deployed

Microsoft emerged as the early leader in the agent platform race. According to Cloud Wars , 160,000 customers have built 400,000 AI agents using the company’s Copilot platform. The scale demonstrates how quickly enterprises are moving beyond experimentation to deployment.

The company announced a range of specialized agents across different domains:

  • Security agents: Six new AI agents for security tasks, including phishing triage that can “handle routine phishing alerts and cyberattacks” and alert fatigue reduction that frees up human defenders
  • Factory automation: New agents for manufacturing environments announced at Hannover Messe 2025
  • Sales agents: AI Accelerator for Sales and new sales agents to accelerate AI-first selling
  • Research and data analysis: OpenAI-powered Copilot agents for workflow acceleration

Microsoft also expanded partnerships: Adobe joined to empower marketers with AI agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot, while OneTrust launched an AI agent built with Microsoft Security Copilot.

ZDNET reported on two new “deep reasoning” AI agents that can speed up workflows. The company is positioning its agents as alternatives to Salesforce CRM systems.

Amazon: Browser Control in Nova Act

Amazon entered the agent platform wars with Nova Act, an AI agent that can directly control web browsers to navigate websites and make purchases. According to The Verge , Amazon’s new agent “is designed to do your shopping.”

The browser-controlling capability represents a significant technical milestone. RetailWire reported that Nova Act “can take over a web browser and make purchases” on behalf of users. As PYMNTS noted , the agent can “shop and place orders” autonomously.

Beyond consumer applications, Amazon Web Services announced general availability of multi-agent collaboration on Bedrock, enabling multiple agents to work together on complex tasks. CNBC reported that the Nova launch “puts it up against rivals OpenAI, Anthropic.”

Salesforce: Agent Marketplace

Salesforce pursued an app store-style strategy with AgentExchange, a marketplace for AI agent skills launched with 200+ initial partners . As Techzine Global reported , the marketplace is “specifically focused on skill-sharing” between agents.

The company also launched Agentforce 2dx, which enables AI agents to run in the background rather than requiring explicit user prompts. According to Techzine Global , the update sets “a new standard” as “AI agents become proactive.”

InfoWorld noted that the update aims to simplify AI agent development and deployment. Salesforce DevOps reported that AgentExchange is designed to “drive adoption of role-based AI agents.”

In healthcare, Salesforce released pre-built AI agents to tackle “time-consuming healthcare tasks.”

Oracle: No-Code Agent Studio

Oracle introduced AI Agent Studio, a no-code tool for creating AI agents across its Fusion application suite. According to Oracle’s announcement , the studio is “available at no additional cost” and delivers “easy-to-use tools, including advanced testing, robust validation, and built-in security.”

ZDNET reported that the new tool is an “impressive next step for Oracle’s AI strategy.” Capacity Global noted that the studio enables businesses to “build custom AI agents.”

Oracle announced AI agents for financial crime detection, adding a “broad class of AI agents and agentic workflows” to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service. SiliconANGLE reported that customers can “create and modify AI agents across” the Fusion suite.

The company also announced general availability of its OCI Generative AI Agents Platform. As Techzine Global noted , Oracle is positioning Agent Studio for Fusion Cloud Applications.

ServiceNow: Pre-Built Agent Library

ServiceNow took a vertical-specific approach with its Yokohama platform release, which adds to “thousands of AI agents across CRM, HR, IT, and more,” according to the Business Wire announcement .

The company introduced AI agents built for the telecom industry . These agents, built with NVIDIA AI Enterprise software and DGX Cloud, are designed to “drive productivity across the entire service lifecycle.”

Diginomica reported that Yokohama is “unleashing pre-configured AI agents, everywhere.” CX Today noted that ServiceNow is “going big on industry-specific innovation” with new AI agents and the Quality 360 acquisition.

Constellation Research reported that the Yokohama release “ups AI agent game” with ServiceNow Studio, an AI-powered workspace for no-code, low-code, and pro-code agent development. Techzine Global noted that ServiceNow is introducing “new AI agents for telecoms.”

Other Platform Players

Several other companies announced agent platforms:

  • PwC launched an AI agent operating system to “revolutionize AI workflows for enterprises”
  • Workato launched its enterprise AI agent platform and acquired AI customer support vendor DeepConverse
  • EY announced the EY.ai Agentic Platform , created with NVIDIA AI, for tax, risk, and finance domains
  • NVIDIA launched a family of open reasoning AI models for building agentic AI platforms
  • Kore.ai announced an agent platform for “building, deploying, and orchestrating agentic applications”
  • WSO2 expanded AI agent capabilities with platform-wide AI-native updates
  • Accenture debuted an AI agent builder within its AI Refinery platform
  • Deloitte unveiled Zora AI , described as “agentic AI for tomorrow’s workforce”
  • Adobe launched the Adobe Experience Platform Agent Orchestrator for businesses to activate AI agents

The Browser Pattern: Agents That Navigate the Web

A clear pattern emerged in March: browser-controlling agents as a primary interface for AI automation.

Browser Use raised $17 million in a funding round to help AI agents navigate websites. As TechCrunch explained , the startup is “making it easier for AI ‘agents’ to navigate websites.” SiliconANGLE reported that the funding will help “steer AI agents through the internet.”

Opera introduced “Browser Operator,” a native AI agent integrated directly into the browser to perform tasks for users. The screenshot from the announcement shows the agent designed to handle web-based workflows without leaving the browser.

Amazon’s Nova Act represents the most ambitious browser-controlling agent to date, with the ability to navigate websites and make purchases directly. The capability matters because it allows agents to interact with existing web infrastructure without requiring API integrations.

However, browser control also creates security concerns. Arcade.dev raised $12 million in seed funding specifically “to solve the biggest security problem with AI Agents.” As the company noted, it is “the first company to help AI agents securely take real-world actions on behalf of a user.”

Security Double-Edged: Agents as Defender and Threat

Agents as Defenders

Microsoft led the charge on using AI agents for security, announcing six specialized security agents for Security Copilot . According to The Verge , the agents will “help overwhelmed humans” by handling routine security tasks.

Help Net Security reported that the new AI agents “take on phishing, patching, alert fatigue.” The phishing triage agent specifically can “handle routine phishing alerts and cyberattacks, freeing up human defenders.”

SailPoint unveiled Harbor Pilot, a set of AI-powered agents for identity security . The agents are designed to “help identity teams work smarter, respond faster and secure their organizations more efficiently.”

Alpha Vision announced it will showcase AI agent-powered security solutions at ISC West 2025, demonstrating how agents can enhance physical security.

Oracle brought AI agents to financial crime detection , adding agents and agentic workflows to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service.

Agents as Attackers

But security researchers also demonstrated how AI agents can be used maliciously. SC Media reported that OpenAI’s Operator AI agent “can be used in phishing attacks.” Researchers showed that the same browser-controlling capabilities that make agents useful for legitimate tasks also enable them to conduct autonomous phishing attacks .

The dual-use nature of agent capabilities creates a security dilemma. As Arcade.dev noted in its funding announcement, securely enabling AI agents to “take real-world actions on behalf of a user” is one of the most critical challenges facing the industry.

Vertical Agents: Healthcare, Finance, and Beyond

Healthcare

Salesforce released pre-built AI agents specifically designed to “tackle time-consuming healthcare tasks.” The agents target administrative workflows that consume provider time.

Wipro announced AI agent solutions for healthcare transformation , powered by Salesforce’s Agentforce platform.

Nature published a paper on “coordinated AI agents for advancing healthcare,” exploring how multi-agent systems can improve medical workflows.

Financial Services

Auquan launched an industry-first AI agent purpose-built for risk monitoring in financial services. As Corporate Compliance Insights noted , Auquan launched an “agentic AI risk agent for FinServ.”

Oscilar announced how it is transforming risk decisioning with AI agents, targeting financial risk assessment workflows.

Oracle expanded its financial crime detection agents , adding a broad class of AI agents to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service.

Other Industries

Telecommunications: ServiceNow introduced AI agents built for the telecom industry , designed to drive productivity across the entire service lifecycle.

Manufacturing: Microsoft launched new AI agents for factory automation at Hannover Messe 2025. Ford is using agents with NVIDIA for distributed inference with collaborative AI agents.

Real Estate: An AI agent claiming to be the “world’s first AI real estate agent” has generated $100M in sales . As The Express Tribune reported , the agent generated $100M in sales for Portugal real estate.

Retail: A Salesforce report found that 75% of retailers say AI agents will be “essential by 2026.” Amazon’s Nova Act directly targets retail shopping workflows.

Infrastructure Funding: Building the Agent Stack

Startup funding in March reveals where the agent ecosystem needs work. Infrastructure startups raised $93.8 million across several categories:

Browser Control & Security

  • Browser Use: Raised $17M for web navigation infrastructure
  • Arcade.dev: Raised $12M to solve agent security problems

Compliance & Payments

  • Norm Ai: Raised $48M for compliance automation agents
  • Paid: Raised $10.8M to “scale financial infrastructure for AI agents”

Specialized Infrastructure

  • Tiga.ai: Raised $2M to launch an AI agent for custom buying signals
  • Nunu.ai: Secured $6M to scale AI agents for game QA testing

Agent Monetization

  • Manny Medina (former Outreach CEO) launched a new startup tackling AI agent monetization. As TechCrunch noted , the startup “helps AI agents get paid.”

Platform Plays

Several consulting firms and platforms launched agent offerings:

  • Powered_by launched the “world’s first AI agency for SMBs” to help small businesses deploy agents
  • Tarka raised funding to arm go-to-market teams with AI agents
  • Oracle announced general availability of its OCI Generative AI Agents Platform
  • Adobe launched Adobe Experience Platform Agent Orchestrator

Reality Check: Why Agents Struggle

Despite the platform launches and funding, critical voices reminded the industry that significant challenges remain.

A widely-cited article titled “Why AI Agents Suck So Bad” detailed frustrating experiences with support agents, highlighting “limitations of current RAG-based AI systems in handling complex customer” issues.

More than half of companies have already deployed autonomous AI agents, according to a study by PagerDuty covered by Quartz. But adoption doesn’t equal satisfaction—implementation challenges abound.

CIO reported that IT leaders are “bracing for the AI agent management challenge.” As organizations deploy more agents, managing them becomes increasingly complex.

Skepticism about “PhD-level” marketing claims continues. As the Indian Express noted , “The hype around PhD-level AI comes with growing scepticism.”

Hidden risks in agent adoption are emerging, including concerns about data silos impacting agent performance. Enterprises face real management complexity as agent deployments scale.

What This Month Means

March 2025 was when AI agents graduated from research project to product. The evidence is across several dimensions:

Pricing as value signal: OpenAI’s reported $20,000 monthly pricing suggests the company believes these systems can deliver substantial enterprise value—even if the “PhD-level” framing remains marketing rhetoric.

Autonomous capabilities are here: China’s Manus demonstrated what fully autonomous agents can do, planning complex tasks without human intervention and drawing comparisons to DeepSeek’s viral impact.

Platform ubiquity: Every major tech company—Microsoft, Amazon, Salesforce, Oracle, ServiceNow—now offers an agent platform. The land grab for enterprise mindshare is underway.

Infrastructure being built: Startup funding of $93.8 million in a single month shows where the ecosystem needs work: browser control, security, payments, compliance, and monitoring.

Enterprise adoption accelerating: Microsoft’s 400,000 agents built by 160,000 customers, the PagerDuty study finding more than half of companies using autonomous agents, and industry-specific deployments all point to real adoption.

But we’re still early. Reliability issues persist, management complexity is real, and the gap between marketing claims and actual capabilities—especially around “PhD-level” performance—remains significant.

The next 6-12 months will be about deployment at scale. Which platforms actually deliver value? Which use cases prove durable? The agent wars have begun, but the winner is far from determined.

Major Agent Platform Launches

Company Platform/Product Key Differentiator Target User
Microsoft Copilot Agents 400,000 agents deployed by 160,000 customers Enterprise
Amazon Nova Act Browser-controlling agent that can shop Consumers & Enterprise
Salesforce AgentExchange Marketplace with 200+ partners Enterprise
Oracle AI Agent Studio No-code creation across Fusion suite Business Users
ServiceNow Yokohama Release Thousands of pre-configured vertical agents Enterprise

Agent Deployments by Industry

Industry Key Players Use Cases Status
Healthcare Salesforce, Wipro Administrative task automation Deployed
Financial Services Auquan, Oscilar, Oracle Risk monitoring, compliance, fraud detection Deployed
Telecom ServiceNow Service lifecycle automation Deployed
Manufacturing Microsoft, Ford Factory automation Deployed
Real Estate Various AI agents Property sales and transactions Deployed
Retail Amazon, Salesforce Shopping automation, customer service Deployed
